lines.text: Painted caves and Roman bridges, kings and revolutions, empire, occupation and liberation. This is the story of France, from Lascaux to the Paris Olympics.
Some seventeen thousand years ago, people deep in a cave in the Dordogne painted horses, stags and bulls. Lascaux holds some of the finest art of the Ice Age.
On the river Seine, a Gallic tribe, the Parisii, made a settlement. It would grow into Paris, a centre of power, art and ideas.
In the last century before the common era, Julius Caesar marched his legions into Gaul and conquered it for Rome.
The Romans left their mark. The Pont du Gard, three tiers of stone fitted without mortar, carried water to Nimes and still stands.
As Rome's power faded, Clovis united the Franks, defeated the last Roman ruler of Gaul, and was baptised a Catholic, a step in the making of France.
In 732 Charles Martel and his Franks turned back a raiding army from the Umayyad Caliphate between Tours and Poitiers.
His grandson Charlemagne conquered much of western Europe, and on Christmas Day in the year 800 the Pope crowned him emperor.
From his empire, in time, came France itself, a kingdom for many centuries, and today a republic with a strong president.
In 843, at Verdun, Charlemagne's three grandsons divided his empire. Its western part is often seen as the beginning of France.
In 987 the Capetian kings took the throne. From a small domain around Paris, their kingdom grew into a great European power.
In 1163 builders began a great Gothic cathedral on an island in the Seine: Notre-Dame de Paris.
In 1337 England and France went to war over the French crown, a struggle that would last more than a century.
Its most famous figure was Joan of Arc, a peasant girl guided by visions, who helped lift the siege of Orleans and was burned at the stake at about nineteen.
Before her time, at Agincourt in 1415, Henry the Fifth's tired English army, with its longbowmen, beat a far larger French force in the mud.
In a calmer age, the philosopher Rene Descartes set out to rebuild knowledge on certainty: I think, therefore I am.
Louis the Fourteenth reigned for seventy-two years, the longest of any European monarch, and gathered power into his own hands.
In 1682 he moved his court to Versailles, whose Hall of Mirrors and vast gardens became the model for palaces across Europe.
In the next century Voltaire mocked the abuses of church and state and argued for free speech and tolerance, the voice of the Enlightenment.
Louis the Sixteenth came to the throne in 1774, with a kingdom deep in debt.
His queen, the Austrian-born Marie Antoinette, was blamed for the court's spending and mocked for her foreign birth.
Far away on Corsica, a boy named Napoleon was born in 1769. Within thirty years he would rule France.
In 1789 the Revolution broke out, and the absolute monarchy and the privileges of the nobility were swept away.
On the fourteenth of July, a Paris crowd stormed the Bastille, the prison that stood for royal power. That day is now France's national day.
Weeks later came the Declaration of the Rights of Man: people are born free and equal in rights, and power comes from the nation.
Then came the Terror. Thousands went to the guillotine, among them the king, the queen, and finally Robespierre himself.
Born in 1802, Victor Hugo would write Les Miserables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, and spend nearly twenty years in exile.
In 1804 Napoleon crowned himself emperor and gave France a single code of law, which still shapes the law of many countries.
His nephew, born in 1808, would one day rule as Napoleon the Third, rebuilding Paris and spreading railways across France.
But in 1815, at Waterloo, Wellington and the Prussians defeated Napoleon for the last time, and he was exiled to Saint Helena.
Louis Pasteur showed that germs cause disease, made vaccines against rabies and anthrax, and gave his name to pasteurisation.
Claude Monet painted Impression, Sunrise, which gave Impressionism its name, then spent years painting the water lilies at Giverny.
In Paris, Marie Curie discovered polonium and radium, and became the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
In 1870 Prussia defeated France and captured Napoleon the Third. The Second Empire was over.
In the spring of 1871, radicals took over Paris as the Commune. In Bloody Week the army crushed it, and thousands were killed.
Coco Chanel, born in 1883, would dress women in simple, comfortable clothes like the little black dress, and launch Chanel Number Five.
For the World's Fair of 1889, an iron tower rose over Paris. The Eiffel Tower was the tallest structure on Earth for forty years.
The next year Charles de Gaulle was born, the soldier who would one day lead the Free French and found a new republic.
In 1894 an army officer, Alfred Dreyfus, was falsely convicted of spying for Germany. The fight over his case divided France until he was cleared.
In a poor district of Paris, Edith Piaf was born in 1915. With La Vie en rose, her voice became a symbol of France.
In 1916 Germany attacked Verdun. France held it for most of the year, at an enormous cost on both sides.
When the war ended, the peace was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, and Germany was made to give up land.
In 1940 France fell. Marshal Petain's government at Vichy worked with the German occupiers, including in the deportation of Jews.
On the sixth of June 1944, Allied troops landed on the beaches of Normandy, the largest seaborne invasion in history.
That August, the Resistance rose in Paris, French and American troops arrived, and four years of occupation ended.
From 1954 France fought Algerian nationalists in a bitter war. It ended in 1962 with Algeria's independence.
Ten years into de Gaulle's Fifth Republic, in May 1968, student protests and a general strike brought France to a standstill.
Zinedine Zidane, born in Marseille in 1972, would lead France to win the World Cup in 1998.
Emmanuel Macron, born in 1977, would become president in 2017 and be re-elected five years later.
In 1981 the first TGV line opened between Paris and Lyon, and high-speed rail spread across Europe.
In 1994 the Channel Tunnel linked France and England by rail, the first fixed crossing since the Ice Age.
In 1999 France joined the euro, and soon its notes and coins replaced the franc.
In January 2015 gunmen attacked the satirical weekly Charlie Hebdo in Paris, killing twelve people, among them its cartoonists.
That November, Islamic State gunmen and bombers struck a concert hall, a stadium and cafes, killing one hundred and thirty people.
In April 2019 fire tore through Notre-Dame, destroying its roof and spire. It was rebuilt and reopened in December 2024.
Less than a year later, a new coronavirus spread across the world, and France, like most countries, went into lockdown.
And in the summer of 2024, Paris opened the Olympic Games with a parade of boats along the Seine, a century after it last hosted them.
From the caves of Lascaux to boats on the Seine, France keeps writing its long story.
